opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've been thinking about for a long time. The way I'd like agents to generalize is the way people do: you drop them into a situation they've never seen and they behave sensibly right away, or adapt within a few attempts. You shouldn't have to retrain them from scratch for every new task.

For a long time in reinforcement learning, the standard approach was to pick one environment, like a single game, and train an agent to master it. You'd get incredible performance, sometimes superhuman, but the agent was incredibly narrow. Change the rules slightly, move some objects around, and it would fall apart. It had learned to solve that particular problem, not anything more general.

What I find exciting is moving away from training on a task and towards training on a whole universe of tasks. If you can procedurally generate a huge, rich space of environments and goals, with different worlds, objectives, and other agents to cooperate or compete with, then the agent can't just memorize solutions. It has to pick up general behaviors: exploring, experimenting, trying something, seeing it fail, and changing strategy. Those are the capabilities that carry over to tasks it has never seen.

The other piece is that the training distribution shouldn't be static. You want the curriculum to adapt to the agent, so it's always facing tasks at the edge of its abilities: not trivially easy, not impossibly hard. That open-endedness, where the learning process keeps generating new challenges, is what I think gets you real generality instead of a collection of narrow skills.

So my ideal is zero-shot, or few-shot, competence on genuinely new tasks, driven by general strategies rather than task-specific tricks. I think that same philosophy, learning from very broad data and structure so you can generalize to new problems, applies well beyond games, including in science.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should show zero-shot or few-shot competence on genuinely new tasks and should not need retraining from scratch.

r002.rationale: It says to train on a “whole universe of tasks” drawn from a huge, rich space of environments and goals.

r003.rationale: It frames training across tasks as the basis for generalization, explicitly contrasting training on one task with training on a universe of tasks.

r004.rationale: It proposes procedurally generating a huge, rich space of environments and goals for training.

r005.rationale: The response does not say that human design capacity limits the complexity of procedurally generated training tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I'd like them to generalize the way a person does when they walk into a new situation: not by having memorized that exact situation, but by having a rich enough repertoire of skills and a good enough model of the world that the new task looks like a recombination of things they already understand.

Concretely, that means a few things. First, the agent shouldn't be trained on one task at a time. If you only ever optimize for a single reward in a single environment, you get something that's exquisitely tuned to that environment and brittle everywhere else. What we found with things like Capture the Flag and later with open-ended environment generation is that if you expose an agent to a huge, procedurally generated distribution of tasks, with goals that are composed out of reusable pieces, then the thing it learns is closer to general competence than to a lookup table. The curriculum matters enormously. You want the agent to always be on the edge of what it can do, so the training signal keeps pushing outward rather than collapsing onto the easy cases.

Second, I'd want generalization to show up at test time without more gradient updates. The agent should be able to read a new goal, or infer one from a few interactions, and then adapt its behavior in context. That's partly a question of representation: does it have an internal notion of objects, agents, and goals that transfers, or has it just learned pixel-to-action reflexes? And it's partly about memory and attention: can it pick up on what's different about this environment in the first few seconds and condition on that?

Third, and this is the part I think people underrate, I want the generalization to be robust to other agents. A lot of the hardest "new tasks" in the real world aren't new because the physics changed, they're new because there's another player with their own strategy. Population-based training and self-play gave us agents that could cope with opponents they'd never seen, because they'd seen a whole ecology of strategies during training rather than one fixed one.

So if I had to compress it: train on distributions, not instances; make the goals compositional so the agent is forced to build reusable abstractions; keep the difficulty adaptive; and make sure the world includes other agents, because that's where the really interesting generalization lives. And then the measure of success is simple. You hand the agent something nobody wrote a reward function for, and it does something sensible.

r001.rationale: The response says it wants generalization at test time without further gradient updates.

r002.rationale: It says agents should be exposed to a huge distribution of tasks rather than trained on a single task.

r003.rationale: It describes training on task distributions and contrasts that with individual instances, identifying tasks as the training examples for cross-task generalization.

r004.rationale: It explicitly proposes a procedurally generated distribution of tasks.

r005.rationale: It does not say human design capacity limits the complexity of tasks that procedural generation can produce.

astra-6.text:
I’d like them to generalize by being able to learn something new, rather than just being able to perform a task they’ve already been trained on. If you put an agent in a new environment, with a new goal, it should bring useful knowledge and skills with it, explore, and use feedback to work out what to do.

So it’s not necessarily about getting the right answer immediately. It’s about adapting efficiently. Can the agent recognize which parts of its previous experience are useful, and which assumptions it needs to change? That’s the kind of generalization I’d really like to see.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should learn and adapt in new environments using feedback; it does not say they should perform well without further training.

r002.rationale: It does not state that generalization across tasks requires many training tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not identify tasks as the units of reinforcement learning training data.

r004.rationale: It does not propose procedural generation for creating training tasks.

r005.rationale: It does not mention human design capacity as a ceiling on task complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like them to generalize in the sense that they can take what they’ve learned and use it to solve a genuinely new problem, without having to start from scratch. That doesn’t necessarily mean doing everything perfectly on the first attempt. It might mean exploring intelligently, figuring out what matters, and learning much faster because of their previous experience.

The exciting thing is an agent that develops useful skills through interaction, then combines and adapts those skills when the task changes. So you’re learning not just a solution to one task, but how to approach a whole range of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response wants agents to use prior experience on new problems, but allows them to learn and adapt on the new task; it does not clearly say they should perform well without further training.

r002.rationale: It does not state that generalizing across tasks requires many training tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not identify tasks as the units of training data.

r004.rationale: It does not propose procedural generation as a way to create training tasks.

r005.rationale: It does not mention human design capacity as a limit on task complexity, including for procedurally generated tasks.
